subtype: Approach: last-minute changes before the event [Pitfall]
passage:
“Jeevan, one more feature. Just a speed boost on the straights. Ten lines,” Parul said at ten p.m. in the lab.
“We haven't tested the current code on the real track since Tuesday.”
“It's tiny. The judges will be impressed.”
“It's the night before.”
“Fine, but let's push it.” Jeevan sighed and typed. They tested it twice on the desk, then packed up.
Next morning, first round. The robot shot forward, missed the first bend and rammed the wall. Parul stared. “The boost. It doesn't switch off at the corner.”
“I told—” Jeevan stopped. “No. It's our code. We can fix it for round two if we can.”
They had ninety seconds to reset. Nobody had saved the old version.

qa.q: Where did the robot go wrong in the first round?
qa.a: The robot missed the first bend and rammed the wall.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the robot failed?
qa.a: Jeevan was frustrated and about to say I told you, but held back and accepted the code was shared.

qa.q: What could the team do differently next time?
qa.a: They could freeze the code the night before, test every change on the real track and keep the old version saved.

qa.q: How might the judges see the first round?
qa.a: The judges see a robot that failed early, and may guess the team took a risk without testing.

grounding: The night before the event the team rewrites the control code to add a feature, never tests it fully and the robot misbehaves in the first round.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: last-minute changes before the event [Pitfall]
passage: The night before the inter-school robotics meet, I had what felt like a brilliant idea. I'm Thomas, and I'd been reading about speed control. Our line-follower was steady but slow. "What if it speeds up on straight lines?" I said to Kashish on a video call at eleven. Kashish yawned. "It works now. Don't touch it." I touched it. By one in the morning I'd rewritten half the control code. I ran it once on the kitchen floor along a straight strip of tape. It flew. I went to bed feeling like a genius. The next morning, on the real track with its sharp curves, our robot shot off the first bend and into the barrier. We lost a full minute putting the old code back. Looking back, one run on a straight line wasn't a test at all.

qa.q: What time did Thomas bring up the idea on the call?
qa.a: At eleven, on a video call with Kashish.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel going to bed that night?
qa.a: Thomas felt excited and overconfident, like a genius, after a single run on a straight strip.

qa.q: What would you change first about how the idea was handled?
qa.a: Save it for after the meet, or test it many times on a copy of the full track with curves, keeping the old code as the default.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel watching the robot hit the barrier?
qa.a: Kashish, who warned against touching working code, may feel frustrated and let down that a late change cost them a full minute.

grounding: Shows a team member rewriting the control code the night before, testing it once, and the robot failing in the first round.

subtype: Approach: last-minute changes before the event [Pitfall]
passage:
Mentor's note, Saturday evening, after round one.
Chetan and Kashish arrived this morning looking tired and oddly proud. They told me they'd added an obstacle-avoid feature last night "for bonus points." I asked whether they had tested it. Chetan said, "Twice. In the hostel corridor." The arena has a shiny floor and bright lights. In round one the robot kept seeing obstacles that weren't there, stopping and turning in circles, and they scored eleven out of forty. Kashish sat on the bench with her head in her hands.
What I did next: I asked them to roll back to Thursday's tested code for round two, and they scored thirty-one. Then we sat down together and wrote a rule on the first page of their notebook: no new features in the last three days, only fixes tested on the real track.

qa.q: What did Chetan and Kashish score in round one?
qa.a: They scored eleven out of forty.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling on the bench?
qa.a: Kashish was upset and discouraged, sitting with her head in her hands after the robot turned in circles.

qa.q: What else could the team have done with the obstacle idea?
qa.a: They could have kept it on a separate copy and tried it under arena-like lighting well in advance, or saved it for the next event.

qa.q: How might Chetan see the switch back to Thursday's code?
qa.a: Chetan may feel embarrassed that the feature failed but relieved when the tested code scored thirty-one, seeing the value of what already worked.

grounding: Illustrates a team adding an untested feature the night before, the robot misbehaving in round one, and the mentor helping them roll back.
